newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW-Penoles plans three mines in '98.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Penoles plans three mines in '98.

text.p: Industrias Penoles, considered the world's largest refined silver producer, said Monday it will open its Herradura mine in first quarter 1998, producing 150,000 equivalent gold ounces per year.
In an interview with Reuters, Penoles said the $73 million investment in the Herradura project in the northwestern state of Sonora is one of the company's top three mine projects.
"It will mark our first incursion into open pit mining," Penoles said, adding production estimates have been revised upwards to 150,000 ounces per year from the original 100,000.
Penoles said Herradura, to be developed jointly with Newmont Gold Co with a 44 percent share holding, had reserves guaranteed for at least a 10-year mine life.

Also, Penoles has set a start-up date of the second half of next year for its Mezcala gold project in the state of Guerrero. Mezcala, a $50 million open pit project also with under development with Newmont, is seen producing 100,000 gold equivalent ounces per year.

Penoles said its third top priority is its Francisco I. Madero zinc project worth $100 million in Zacatecas state. "We expect it to have an output of 90,000 tonnes of zinc concentrate per year over a life of 10 years," Penoles said.

La Oroya is a three circuit (copper, lead and zinc) metallurgic complex lying in Peru's central Andes at 12,300 feet (3,700 metres) above sea level, some 120 miles (190 km) east of Lima. The complex of refineries and smelters processes 22 metals and byproducts.

Penoles said it would bid in Peruvian government auctions of mines. "We are looking for integration," Penoles said, adding a company-wide goal was to increase own-mine intakes to feed into metal complexes.

Plans are to bid in the upcoming auction for the Mahr Tunel mines in Peru, another segment of the huge state-owned miner Centromin that is coming on the block. Mahr Tunel controls the San Cristobal and Andaychagua mines in the Andes -- only around 30 miles (50 km) from the La Oroya complex.
Penoles said the company would make a decision soon on how to finance development at La Oroya. Options include setting up an international division and using the current Met-Mex division.

On financing, Penoles said the company would continue its time-honored strategy of raising money for each specific project. "We believe in direct financing, handing the money over to each project to make sure each project is financially viable," Penoles said, saying the company prefers direct bank credits rather than issuing bonds.

Penoles pointed to the company's recent financing of its Tizapa and La Cienaga mines, via the Japanese commercial banking sector and UBS resepctively, as examples that will be followed. "These other projects are going to see the same financing story," Penoles said.

On output, Penoles declined to give forecasts for silver, gold, lead and zinc production for 1997. "We do not give forecasts, all we can say is that we aiming to achieve at least levels produced last year if not higher," Penoles added.
Penoles, one of Mexico's most traditional companies, has a policy to speak as a company entity and not with an individual voice of a director or spokesman.
